result.final_text:
## What this letter says
You were in hospital with pneumonia (a lung infection). It did not get better with treatment at home.

Doctors think it may be a viral type (atypical pneumonia). This is possible, not certain. The lung doctor was not sure of the exact cause.

Your oxygen was low (hypoxia) before you came in. Later it got better.

Your fever broke 18 hours before you left hospital. Your strength also got better.

A chest x-ray showed mild patchy marks in the lungs. A CT scan showed no specific focal problem.

You have rheumatoid arthritis. Doctors suspect mild adrenal insufficiency from stress. This is possible, not certain. It means the adrenal glands may not make enough of their hormones.

One test is still pending: the C. difficile toxin test. The result is not known yet.

Methotrexate is known to cause lung inflammation (pneumonitis) on some occasions.

You had a reaction to Avelox. Augmentin caused loose stools.

## What you need to do
1. Finish your azithromycin. You have 2 pills left at home.
2. Follow up with Dr. X (the lung doctor) in two to three days.
3. Continue the higher dose of prednisone, 20 mg.

## Dates and medicines
- Follow-up with Dr. X: in two to three days.
- Last dose of Remicade: June.
- Azithromycin: you were continued on it in hospital. The dose is not stated. You have 2 pills left.
- Rocephin (by IV): 1 g daily. You had it before and during your hospital stay. The letter does not say if it continues after you leave.
- Prednisone: 20 mg per day. This is higher than before (5 mg per day).
- Methotrexate: 20 mg every week. It was held (not taken) this past Friday. The hospital will ask your rheumatologist (joint doctor) if you should continue it. This is not decided yet.
- Remicade: every eight weeks.

## Questions to ask your doctor
- When will I get my C. difficile test result?
- Will I keep taking Rocephin after I leave hospital?
- Should I take methotrexate again?
- How long do I take the higher dose of prednisone?

## When to get urgent help
The letter does not list specific warning signs.

If you are worried and it is not an emergency, call NHS 111. In an emergency, call 999.

---
*This explanation was made by a computer program to help you read your letter. It may contain mistakes. It does not replace your doctor, nurse or pharmacist. Always follow the letter and ask them if anything is unclear.*
